title: A new king (Exodus 1:8–14)
hookLine: a Pharaoh who didn't know Joseph fears the Hebrews and enslaves them

cards: A new book. Jews call it Shemot, names, after its opening words: these are the names of the sons of Israel who came into Egypt. Christians call it Exodus, the Greek word for the way out.
It starts where Genesis left off. Joseph dies. His brothers die.
That whole generation dies. And their children are fruitful and multiply, the text says, until the land is filled with them. A family that came down for bread has become a people.
Then comes one sentence, and the whole story turns on it.

teach.h: A NEW KING, WHICH KNEW NOT JOSEPH.
teach.b: In the King James Bible: "Now there arose up a new king over Egypt, which knew not Joseph." A generation passes, and someone forgot: the man who saved Egypt from famine, and why these people were here at all.
Forgetting makes room for fear. The new king tells his people: these Israelites are more and mightier than we are. Let's deal wisely with them, or if a war comes, they'll join our enemies.

It's an old move: call your neighbors a threat, and act before they can do anything. So the Egyptians set taskmasters over them, to wear them down with heavy labor. They build store cities for Pharaoh, Pithom and Raamses.

teach.h: FEAR: THEY ARE MORE THAN WE.
teach.b: "But the more they afflicted them, the more they multiplied and grew." The plan backfires, so the oppression tightens.
The Egyptians made their lives bitter with hard bondage, in mortar and brick and all kinds of work in the field.
Bitter will come back: Exodus later tells Israel to eat the Passover with bitter herbs, and Jews still eat them at the Seder.
Notice what Exodus doesn't say. It never names this Pharaoh. Historians have proposed different kings, and some doubt we can place the story in Egyptian records at all.
The book seems less interested in which king than in what kind. Exodus is a story of God hearing people who cry out, and it starts with a ruler who didn't remember.

how: Christians read Exodus as the story of God hearing the cry of the oppressed (Exodus 2:23–25; 3:7), and some churches draw on its opening chapters when they pray about forced labor and trafficking today.

games.q: you're the new king of Egypt. a foreign people in your land has grown large. you don't remember why they came. what do you do?
o: honor them for what their ancestor did for Egypt.
call them a threat and put them to forced labor.
games.why: he says they are more and mightier than we, sets taskmasters over them, and makes their lives bitter. it began with forgetting.

practice: Look at the things around you, your clothes, your phone, the food in your kitchen: somewhere in the chains that made them, there may be people working who are not free to leave.
You don't know their names; picture them anyway, tired hands, bricks of their own. If you pray, you can pray for them; if you don't, hold them in mind, and let yourself remember them.
